name: Erik Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent Brookfold Farm, about 160 hectares, from a pension fund that's never once set foot on it. Most days start at six with the sheep, around 600 ewes, then whatever the barley needs, then fixing whatever broke yesterday. My tractor's a 1998 Ford I keep alive with parts from a scrapyard in Kellby. I like lambing, honestly, even the nights. What I don't like is the paperwork and the rent review letters.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The landlord's agent, a young lad called Pryce with a tablet. He walks the fields twice a year and talks about yield per hectare like the ewes are a spreadsheet. My partner Lena works as a teaching assistant, so we get by, but the tenancy is up for renewal in 2028 and that sits in my stomach. Noah's twelve and Ivy's nine, and they both think the farm is ours. It isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's the one I'd pick if anyone asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the mart: told you so. All this talk about robots in the fields and it turned out to be another gadget for the people who already had money. I'd probably put a smug comment under the farmers' union post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I keep my head down and keep paying rent that goes up every three years anyway. AI was never the real problem for me. The problem is that the land belongs to people who don't farm it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm doing. Lamb in March, shear in June, sell the barley through the co-op store in Kellby. Maybe I'd finally replace the gearbox on the Ford, about 2,000 if I can find a used one. I'd keep going to union meetings because the rent fight doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. A bit of me would also feel daft for how much I worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the AI tools that did turn up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Lena uses one to write school reports and she says it's handy, fine, good for her. I don't want a machine telling me when a ewe's going to lamb when I can see it in the ewe's eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real problem is ownership. Would the union fight look different in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, and that's sort of the point. It'd be the same fight we've had since my grandad's time. Tenants against landlords, small against big.

S0.say: I told you so. All this talk about robots in the fields, and it turned out to be another gadget for the people who already had money.
S0.think: AI was never my real problem. The problem is that the land I work belongs to a pension fund that puts the rent up every three years.
S0.do: Carries on with the same calendar of lambing, shearing and selling barley through the co-op. Replaces the tractor gearbox for about 2,000 if he can find one used, and keeps going to union meetings.
S0.feel: Relief, with a little embarrassment about how much he worried.
S0.quote: I don't want a machine telling me when a ewe's going to lamb when I can see it in the ewe's eyes.
S0.fieldNote: Erik turned the conversation to land ownership almost straight away. For him, technology is a side issue next to who owns the farm. He refuses AI tools even when they're harmless, and seems proud of that.

steps.text: Lamb in March, shear in June and sell the barley through the Kellby co-op
Replace the 1998 Ford tractor's gearbox if a used one turns up for about 2,000
Keep going to farmers' union meetings, because the tenants' rent fight goes on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one's closer to what I actually see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it needs rules. If the big estates get robot sprayers and drone shepherds, the tenants get squeezed out, and someone in government has to stop that. I'd say that at the union branch and I'd sign whatever petition goes round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Pryce would love it. A robot-run farm doesn't ask for a new roof on the lambing shed. If the fund can merge Brookfold with the next two farms and run it with one manager and a fleet of machines, they'll do it at the 2028 renewal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting away an extra 150 a month, which hurts, and we'd skip the summer week at Lena's sister's caravan. I'd push the union branch to bring a tenant rights motion to the regional meeting by spring. And I'd write to our local representative, which I've never done, asking for long tenancies to be protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but it's like hearing a noise in the engine you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the new machines yourself, to make yourself harder to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I should say yes. But I'm 43 and I've never even used one of those chat things, and I don't want to start learning to babysit a robot that's there to replace me. Maybe if the union ran a course and paid for the time, I'd go. Maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noah and Ivy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing yet. Noah asked me last month if he'd get the farm one day and I said we'll see. I'd keep saying we'll see until I actually know.

S1.say: This needs rules. If the big estates get robot sprayers and drone shepherds, the tenants get squeezed out, and someone in government has to stop that.
S1.think: A robot-run farm doesn't ask for a new roof on the lambing shed. If the fund can merge Brookfold with the next two farms and run it with machines, they'll do it at the 2028 renewal.
S1.do: Saves an extra 150 a month and cancels the family's summer week away. Pushes his union branch to table a tenant rights motion by spring and writes to his local representative for the first time.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing an engine noise he can't place.
S1.quote: I don't want to start learning to babysit a robot that's there to replace me.
S1.fieldNote: Erik admits he probably should learn the new machines, then refuses anyway. His fear is not the robots themselves but what the landowner can do with them. He's keeping the truth from his son with 'we'll see'.

steps.text: Put away an extra 150 a month and skip the summer caravan week
Push the union branch to take a tenant rights motion to the regional meeting by spring
Write to the local representative for the first time, asking to protect long tenancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's the year my tenancy's up. Of course it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the mart that the machines can think now but they still can't lamb a ewe at two in the morning, so the fight isn't lost yet. At the union branch I'd say we've got three years before the robots, and we'd better use every one of them. I'd want a law on the books before 2031, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking part of farming was never my part. Pryce's part is, the yield tables and the rent reviews, and that's the part a computer takes over in 2028. So at the renewal the fund gets a perfect report on Brookfold from a machine, and I think they'd offer me three years instead of the usual ten. Just long enough to keep the sheep alive until the robots can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the 2028 renewal with the union's solicitor, not on my own, and fight for a full ten-year term. We'd stop the extra 150 a month going on anything but savings, and Lena's pay would cover the food. I'd put my name down for the union's tenant committee and go to the regional meeting in person. I still wouldn't use the AI for the subsidy forms, though Lena would probably do them on her laptop whether I liked it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being told the date of an operation. Three years sounds like plenty until you count lambings, and that's only three lambings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the thinking work goes first. Would anything about your own day change in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork would, and that's the bit I hate, so you'd think I'd be pleased. The subsidy forms would fill themselves in, the vet's records would sort themselves out. But the hands on the ewes would still be mine for three more years, and then they wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noah if the fund only gave you three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noah would be fourteen by then and he'd see the letter on the table. I'd tell my son the truth for once, that the farm was never ours and now it's on a timer. Then I'd ask him what he actually wants to do, because I've never asked.

S2.say: The machines can think now, but they still can't lamb a ewe at two in the morning, so the fight isn't lost yet. We've got three years before the robots, and we need a law before 2031.
S2.think: The thinking work that goes first is the agent’s side of farming, not mine, and it hands the fund a perfect report on Brookfold right at the 2028 renewal. I think they’d offer me three years instead of ten, just long enough to keep the sheep alive until the robots can do it.
S2.do: Takes the union's solicitor to the 2028 renewal to fight for a ten-year term, and puts the extra 150 a month straight into savings. Joins the union's tenant committee and goes to the regional meeting, while still refusing AI for the subsidy forms.
S2.feel: Like being told the date of an operation. Three years sounds long until he counts it as three lambings.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son the truth for once, that the farm was never ours and now it's on a timer.
S2.fieldNote: The three-year gap matters to Erik, but mostly as a countdown, not a cushion. He sees right away that thinking AI hits the landlord's side of farming first and gives the fund what it needs to plan his exit. The paperwork he hates would vanish, and he still wouldn't touch the tool that does it.

steps.text: Take the union's solicitor to the 2028 tenancy renewal and push for ten years
Put the extra 150 a month into savings and live on Lena's pay for food
Tell Noah the farm isn't theirs and ask what he really wants to do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the renewal in 2028 comes and goes before any of it. That's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before, we need the rules in place while there's time. Five years for the thinking machines and eight for the robots is a long enough runway for a law if anyone in government bothers. I'd say it at the union branch and I'd say it to our local representative's face this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd sign the 2028 renewal and feel like I'd got away with something. Then the 2031 renewal would be the one with the computer report attached, and the fund would offer me three years to 2034. I'd be 51 by the time the robots came, which is too young to stop and too old to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the 2028 renewal for as long as they'd give me, ten years if the union can get it, before the fund's AI is in the picture. I'd keep the extra 150 a month going into savings for all five years, and I'd stand for branch secretary. I'd still fix the Ford instead of buying anything clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then anxious when I do the sums. Getting past one renewal feels good for about a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 51 when the robots came. What work would you look for then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about the council's verges and hedges, the ones round Kellby. That's outdoor work, and a council might be slower to buy robots than a pension fund. But I don't know that, and I'd hate to bet my kids' school shoes on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lena's job be safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching assistant, with kids who need a grown-up beside them? I'd think so, longer than mine. Lena keeping her job at the school is what would let me sleep at all. Funny, I always thought of the farm as the main income.

S3.say: We need the rules in place while there's time. Five years for the thinking machines and eight for the robots is long enough for a law if anyone in government bothers.
S3.think: I’d sign the 2028 renewal and feel like I’d got away with something, but the 2031 renewal would come with the computer report attached and a three-year offer. I’d be 51 when the robots came, too young to stop and too old to start over.
S3.do: Signs the 2028 renewal for as long as he can get, ideally ten years with union help, before the fund's AI is in the picture. Keeps saving the extra 150 a month for five years and stands for branch secretary of the farmers' union.
S3.feel: Uneasy at first, then anxious when he does the sums. Getting past one renewal feels good for about a day.
S3.quote: I’d be 51 by the time the robots came, which is too young to stop and too old to start over.
S3.fieldNote: Erik spotted at once that this timing puts his 2028 renewal before the AI arrives, and his plan hangs on locking in a long term then. He still won't retrain or buy machines. His real safety net, he admitted, is Lena's job at the school.

steps.text: Sign the 2028 Brookfold renewal for the longest term the union can win
Keep saving the extra 150 a month for all five years
Press the local representative in person for a law protecting farm tenants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years before a robot can lamb. I'd be 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse now. Ten years for the thinking machines and thirteen for the robots, so if tenants get thrown off in 2039 it's because nobody made the rules. I'd keep saying it at every branch meeting until someone got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd get two more renewals and the kids would be grown. Ivy would be in her twenties by 2039. The bit that keeps me up is being 56 with no farm and ten years before any pension, but that's a long way off and I'm good at not thinking about long way offs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on farming the same way and not buy any robot. I'd help Noah into an apprenticeship that isn't farming, maybe with the electricians in Kellby, and I'd want Ivy to stay in school as long as she likes. I'd keep a bit going into savings each month, but not the full 150, because ten years is too long to live that tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a worry I can put in a drawer. I'd take it out at renewal time and put it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the paperwork side change before the robots came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2036, sure, the forms and the rent reports would all be the computer's job. I'd probably have given in by then and let Lena set something up for the subsidy claims. I've said no to things before and ended up using them, like the mobile phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep farming the same way. Doesn't the warning change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes it for the kids, not for me. I'd fight for everyone else's future in a meeting room and then go home and do the evening feed like always. Not proud of it, but that's me.

S4.say: There's no excuse now. If tenants get thrown off in 2039, it's because nobody bothered to make the rules in the thirteen years they had.
S4.think: I think I’d get two more renewals and the kids would be grown by the time the robots came. Being 56 with no farm and years before a pension scares me, but it’s far enough off that I can push it aside.
S4.do: Carries on farming as before without buying any robot, and steers Noah toward a non-farming apprenticeship, perhaps with the Kellby electricians. Keeps saving a smaller amount each month rather than the full 150, since ten years is too long to live that tight.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, with a worry he can put in a drawer and take out at renewal time.
S4.quote: I'd fight for everyone else's future in a meeting room and then go home and do the evening feed like always.
S4.fieldNote: With thirteen years before robots, Erik relaxes and points the warning at his children instead of himself. He admits he usually gives in to new technology late, like the mobile phone. The gap between his union speeches and his own habits is something he names himself.

steps.text: Keep farming the 600 ewes and barley without buying any robot
Help Noah into a non-farming apprenticeship, perhaps with the Kellby electricians
Save a smaller monthly sum than 150 so the family isn't living tight for ten years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest. The thinking machines land the same year my tenancy does, and the fund would give me three years until the robots, then nothing. What would help is a law that says you can't end a farm tenancy just to put robots on it, and some kind of income for people like me while we work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks if the robots can do the work. Nobody asks who gets the money when they do.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if the robots can do the work. Nobody asks who gets the money when they do.
portrait: Erik Quinn, 43, rents Brookfold Farm from a pension fund and runs about 600 ewes and some barley with a 1998 tractor he keeps alive himself. He never uses AI and refuses to start, seeing the real problem as land ownership rather than technology. He is calm if AI stalls and uneasy at steady change. Fast AGI alarms him because the thinking machines arrive at his 2028 renewal and he expects only three years before robots replace him; with slower timelines he plans to lock in a long tenancy early, pins his hopes on the union and Lena's school job, and points the extra time at his children's futures rather than his own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the thinking machines arrive at his tenancy renewal and he expects only three years before robots take the farm work.
whatWouldHelp: A law stopping landlords ending farm tenancies just to automate, and an income for people like him while they work out what's next.
